Honors contracts are formal agreements, facilitated by an honors program, between a student and instructor.
They allow students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an honors level through additional learner-directed work tailored to the “broader, deeper, and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC); and WHEREAS, contracts are recognized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership by enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kansas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.

They can “facilitate access to honors, increases completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with structured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences”; and WHEREAS, honors contracts may be best understood as a form of an independent study, entered into voluntarily by both students and faculty, with a contract defining outcomes, deadlines, and assessment definitions for additional work related to the course materials; and WHEREAS, honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals.
They also allow programs to meet student needs when student/faculty constraints or funding limitations preclude offering stand-alone honors courses that fit student interests and needs; and WHEREAS, Contracts provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions such as ours that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough student body to fill honors sections.

Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for the self-guided intellectual growth of students; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Faculty Senate of the University of Rhode Island calls for implementation of the following Honors Contracts Proposal.

recommended changes to the University Catalog and to the eCampus system used by Enrollment Services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Honors Program is called upon to reflect these changes on their website and in all other promotional and outreach materials promulgated by the Program. UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE 2006-07-5 March 1, 2007 ESTABLISHMENT OF THE STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES OVERSIGHT COMMITTEE BACKGROUND: The Student Learning Improvement Assessment Advisory Committee (SLIAAC) is an ad hoc committee formed in 2005 by the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, with representation from all colleges and Student Affairs.
SLIACC has 27 members and meets approximately monthly.
The size of the committee has been productive in the examination of the implications and implementation of outcomes assessment.
At this time, the ad hoc committee has agreed that a standing joint committee on learning outcomes assessment should be established to continue the work of the ad hoc committee.
They have forwarded a proposal to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee for consideration.
In consultation with the Provost and the Ad Hoc Student Learning Improvement Assessment Advisory Committee, the Executive Committee proposes the establishment of a joint Learning Outcomes Oversight Committee (LOOC).

Proposal: Committee Structure: The Committee would be a Joint Committee of the Faculty Senate and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs.
The proposed structure best represents a shared governance approach to student learning outcomes assessment, increasing the likelihood of policy change and implementation, as well as a firmer connection with the University’s administration.
Such a structure ensures that resource requirements for advancing the effective assessment of learning outcomes could be directly addressed.
This structure also would provide a more unified voice for addressing constituencies outside the University, including strategic handling of data.
In addition, other areas critical to overall student outcomes, such as co-curricular activities and initiatives, would be given an appropriate voice.
It is the recommendation of this ad hoc committee that the Joint Committee be heavily represented by faculty, with broad representation of the colleges and a faculty member who will serve as Chair.
